docs.title: ML in PL Workshops
docs.text:
Teams often suffer from conventions, domain knowledge and unwritten assumptions live only in the developers’ heads. This hands-on workshop sends you home with a shareable engineering methodology your team can adopt to standardize coding, make engineers benefit from Subject Matter Experts insights (as well as the other way around).

We will teach you how to apply classic software engineering principles to agentic coding: separation of concerns, dependency management and design patterns. Starting from a provided template, you will build, test, and install your own package ready to distribute across your team and with best practices baked into the design.

docs.title: Goals of the tutorial
docs.text:
• Objective: present an emerging methodology for agentic coding along with practical examples on a specific tool.
  • Attendee benefit: Learn vocabulary, patterns, tools and methodology for efficient coding. Benefit from codified coding standards and be able to focus on the domain challenges more. Be able to hassle-free exchange prompts in your team and across teams in your company.
  • Learning outcomes: participants know how to create their own package, understand primitives, are familiarised with the methodology around instrumented codebase design (good practices, anti-patterns, vocabulary, design patterns, tools, resources).
  • Prerequisites: Nice to have: familiarity with dependency management, software design patterns, and object-oriented programming. Required: understanding of core LLM concepts such as attention, the context window, and the “lost in the middle” phenomenon. Participants should bring a CLI for the coding agent of their choice, compatible with APM (e.g. GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, Codex, Gemini/Antigravity, Windsurf), and a GitHub account.

docs.title: Attribution and resources used
docs.text: For the sources used in this tutorial as well as further steps please see the part 4: Further resources and next steps.

docs.title: Intro: Fundamental concepts, methodology
docs.text:
This part aims to give you the vocabulary and theoretical background before jumping right into creating your own skills. Based on the provided methodology you will be able to make conscious choices about the design of your primitives.

graph LR
    subgraph Intro["Now: Introduction and theory"]
        package-org["APM"]
        dp["Design patterns"]
        audit["Instrumentation audit"]
    end

    subgraph Other["Latter"]
        exercises["Hands-on exercises"]
        wrap-up["Wrap-up and resources"]
    end

    Intro --> exercises
    exercises --> wrap-up

We cover the following:

  1. The tools that help with distribution, portability, validation, and governance.

  2. Design patterns for primitives structure and content.

  3. A repository audit methodology tailored for research and PoC repositories.

docs.title: Design patterns
docs.text:
Design patterns are typical solutions to commonly occurring problems in software design. They are like pre-made blueprints that you can customize to solve a recurring design problem in your code. 1 You may know some famous patterns like Strategy, Facade or Factory.

It turns out that there is an equivalent concept for agentic primitives (which also strengthens the idea that we should treat agentic primitives as code, not as part of documentation).

graph LR
    classical["Classic design patterns"]
    agentic["Agentic design patterns"]

    classical -- "Concepts transferred" --> agentic

An agentic design pattern is a reusable solution to coordination challenges in LLM driven systems where execution paths are decided at runtime rather than hardcoded in advance. While traditional software patterns assume deterministic components and static control flow, agentic patterns coordinate probabilistic models that dynamically invoke tools, revise intermediate results, or hand off work to other agents. 2

Only selected architectural patterns and anti-patterns for agentic workflows are presented. For the full pattern catalogue see the resources used.

Vocabulary Alert

Some of the design pattern names may seem like buzzwords and overwhelming jargon at first. But after familiarizing yourself with them, they provide a robust vocabulary making conversations richer, going beyond "I told Claude to make it work, make no errors."

docs.title: Tiers of patterns
docs.text:
graph TD
    R["Refactor patterns"]
    A["Tier 3: architectural patterns"]

    subgraph Tier2["Tier 2: design patterns"]
        C["Creational"]
        S["Structural"]
        B["Behavioral"]
    end

    H["Tier 1: harness idioms"]
    P["Tier 0: substrate primitives"]

    R --> A
    A --> C
    A --> S
    A --> B
    C --> H
    S --> H
    B --> H
    H --> P

Patterns from Tier 3 are composed of Tier 2 patterns. For example, the A1. PANEL is represented as:

\[ \text{A1 PANEL} = \text{B1} + N \times \text{C2} + \text{S4} + \text{B4} \]

Where:

  • \(\text{B1}\) (Fan-out and synthesizer): coordinates fan-out topology and synthesis.
  • \(N \times \text{C2}\) (Persona preload): instantiates \(N\) specialized review lenses in isolated contexts.
  • \(\text{S4}\) (Validation decorator): gates the synthesized verdict.
  • \(\text{B4}\) (Plan memento): persists the deliberation outcome to storage.
Pattern family Primary responsibility R (Refactor) Module boundary hygiene, decomposing monoliths A (Architectural) Multi-agent execution graphs, macro flows C (Creational) Context isolation, persona scoping, lazy assets S (Structural) Deterministic tool bridges, validation gates B (Behavioral) Dynamic coordination, attention anchoring, plan memory

docs.title: Primitive relations
docs.text:
APM packages structure capabilities into distinct relation types:

graph TD
    subgraph Package["Local package"]
        Inline["Inline skill"]
        SiblingSkill["Sibling skill"]
        Asset["Sibling asset"]
        Subagent["Sibling subagent"]
    end

    External["External package"]

    User(["User"]) -->|"Invokes"| Inline
    User -.->|"Direct dispatch"| SiblingSkill
    Inline -->|"Delegates to"| SiblingSkill
    Inline -->|"Loads on demand"| Asset
    Inline -->|"Spawns child thread"| Subagent
    Subagent -->|"Runs CLI or script"| Tools["System tools"]
    External -.->|"Reused via apm.yml"| Inline
  • Inline: Content and logic that live directly within the primitive's own file, executing in the active session context with no dependency edges.
  • Sibling: Primitives (such as specialized skills, lazy assets, or child subagents) colocated in the same local package, referenced on demand or dispatched independently without crossing distribution boundaries.
  • External: Upstream packages pulled from external repositories and pinned via apm.yml, crossing distribution boundaries for multi-project reuse.
  • Other (Runtime tool affordances): Deterministic execution bridges (CLI utilities, compilers, scripts) that are runtime mechanisms rather than prompt primitives, invoked by subagents to interact with the system environment.

docs.title: Fun fact: Caveman
docs.text:
Caveman 3 project proposed the idea of saving tokens by making the agent talk like a caveman. Thus simplifying the language and cutting tokens aggressively.

The behavioral patterns formalize the Caveman concept, especially for agent-agent communication. The Caveman channel (B14b/c) uses high-density briefs and structured JSON receipts:

graph TD
    Parent["Parent orchestrator"]
    Child["Child subagent"]

    Parent -- "Telegraphic brief (~80 tokens)" --> Child
    Child -- "Runs deterministic tool" --> Child
    Child -- "JSON receipt (~40 tokens)" --> Parent
  • Spawn brief: Drops articles and politeness; retains exact paths, commands, and constraints.
  • Receipt: Minimal JSON object (status, artifact_path, error_digest) keeping parent context clean.

  1. Alexander Shvets, "What's a Design Pattern?", Refactoring Guru. ↩

  2. Molisha Shah, "What Are Agentic Design Patterns? 2026 Pattern Catalog", Augment Code, 2026. ↩

  3. Julius Brussee, "caveman-code", GitHub. ↩

docs.title: Code instrumentation audit of a research codebase
docs.text: The instrumentation audit is a methodology for evaluating the knowledge (often implicit) your research depends on, rather than the scripts or notebooks themselves. The idea is to add a layer of context to the codebase.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
The justification for messy research code is shrinking. We can define standards before prototyping instead of wasting time on review, fixing, and debugging.

Imagine a scenario:

  1. A Subject Matter Expert (SME) is contributing to a repository.

  2. The SME has deep domain knowledge, but basic coding skills.

  3. There is a classical Software Engineer on the team with no domain knowledge, but strong coding skills.

Now consider two scenarios. In the first, there is no codebase instrumentation. In the second, standards, preferences, and implicit knowledge are codified into agentic primitives. In both situations the SME is tasked to implement a new feature.

docs.title: Failure mode
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    actor ENG as Engineer
    actor SME
    participant EXP as Experiment implementation<br/>(no standards)
    participant REV as Review

    Note over ENG: Present, but defines no standards
    SME->>EXP: Implements experiment
    EXP->>REV: Messy research code
    Note over REV: Slow review, fixing, debugging
    REV-->>SME: Rework requests
    REV-->>ENG: Untangle and rewrite
    EXP-->>EXP: Domain insights lost in prints
    ENG->>ENG: Fixes the same issues again, no compounding

This is the default mode. Write code first, correct if required.

docs.title: Success scenario
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    actor ENG as Engineer
    box SME context
        actor SME
        participant EXP as Experiment implementation<br/>(standards applied)
    end
    participant REV as Review

    ENG->>EXP: Defines standards before prototyping<br/>(logger, project structure, abstract classes, typing)
    SME->>EXP: Implements experiment, standards enforced by default<br/>(logger instead of print)
    EXP->>REV: Production ready code
    Note over REV: Faster review, no cleanup
    EXP-->>EXP: Domain insights
    ENG->>ENG: Improves standards

Code is written in alignment with team standards. SMEs who do not care as much about coding can benefit from the abstractions and tooling without learning every detail by heart.

A researcher aiming to obtain experiment results can be viewed as an SME. We can apply the same rule to research projects: instrument the codebase beforehand, accelerate research and development, and avoid paying the cost later on right before a conference submission.

docs.title: Step 1: List your conventions
docs.text: This step is often a bottleneck because conventions are not yet defined.

docs.title: What are the repeatable steps in almost every research repository?
docs.text:
1. Research lab standard: repository setup.
  2. Justifying each design choice (a research log). Record every experiment: goal, hypothesis, method, results, analysis, and next steps, including failures.
  3. Code audit before release: removing unused experiments, dead comments, and duplicated code.
  4. Code, dataset, model, and paper release. Doing this manually incurs a recurring time cost; automation is a one-time cost.
  5. Creating a demo on Hugging Face or a research project website (using templates like this academic project page template as a baseline).

docs.title: Anti-patterns specific to research repositories
docs.text:
1. Missing requirements.txt or lock file, with an unspecified Python version.
  2. Duplicated code (to reduce it, enforce the rule: use, don’t reimplement), often due to missing or insufficient abstractions.
  3. Overused type hints.
  4. Stale notebooks that are no longer relevant to ongoing development.
  5. Dead code.
  6. Test files scattered across source code modules.
  7. Flat project structure (avoiding moving modules like models/, pipeline/, utils/, etc. to src/).
  8. Outdated README or documentation.

Some of these anti-patterns were a necessary evil in rapid research prototypes. Agents can now maintain them smoothly, provided standards are defined.

docs.title: Vague requirements: are research repos truly unique?
docs.text: I do not believe most research projects are fundamentally unique in structure. While the core scientific insight is unique, almost every project ingests data, runs scripts or notebooks, conducts experiments, and publishes results. A research project is like a kebab: you have the scientific meat, but you benefit greatly from an engineering pita.

docs.title: Step 2: Classify each convention item
docs.text:
Once existing conventions are listed, classify them. Where do they come from? Are there existing artifacts that we can reuse? Do we need to codify word-of-mouth knowledge first?

Location Meaning Agent visibility In heads Known by team members, never written down Completely invisible In code Expressed in types, naming, structure Visible if in context window In literature Preexisting papers, datasets, models, terminology that may impact our research Invisible unless explicitly loaded Lab/conference guidelines or reviewer feedback Implicit conventions, known by lab members or documented outside the repository Invisible unless explicitly loaded In data / experiment tracking tools Formats, sources, targets, and schemas Invisible unless explicitly loaded In docs Repository documentation or external guides (e.g., Athena cluster docs) Invisible unless explicitly loaded

docs.title: Step 3: Rank by failure cost
docs.text:
• Critical: Blocks experiment progress, slows down collaboration between team members, makes debugging harder, and slows iterations. Completed experiments cannot be justified without repeating the entire reasoning process to understand why they were run. Data leakage, silent non-determinism, and broken train/test splits.
  • High: Leads to reproducibility issues for other researchers. Notebook sprawl, duplicated experiment code, and bloated repositories (burning tokens due to exploding repository size).
  • Medium: Running additional experiments after review taxes the team by requiring a return to a messy codebase.
  • Low: Style preferences that do not affect correctness.

Issues common in enterprise software (such as technical debt, security vulnerabilities, and production outages) are rarely the primary concern for typical research repositories.

docs.title: Step 4: Map each item to a primitive type
docs.text: If the knowledge... It belongs in... Concrete research example Is a rule scoped to specific files/directories An instruction file Jupyter notebook conventions Requires specialist expertise or a specific model An agent configuration Stronger model for experiment design, cheaper model for implementation Applies across files and needs a decision framework A skill Implementing a new model for evaluation Defines a repeatable multi-step process A prompt Releasing code, models, datasets, or packages Records a decision, trade-off, or historical fact A memory file Design decision justifications, research log Specifies a feature with components and success criteria A specification Experiment plan Defines an automated response to a development event A hook Automated paper, model, or dataset release

docs.title: Step 5: Write your starter set
docs.text: Implement the first primitive. Start small and add primitives gradually.

docs.title: Why even use APM?
docs.text:
Before apm the skills were published per harness. Moreover, the installation was either manual download or via npm. Considering that nowadays repositories with skills can easily reach 100k+ github stars they definitely deserve a customized tool for managing them. This section goes over the reasons why APM is worth using as well as how to define the most frequeltly used primitives. 1

The irony of GitHub stars distribution

The irony is that apm has less than 4k stars and remains a niche while skills like grillme go viral. We highly recommend to leave a star for the APM repo and the other resources we mention during the tutorial!

docs.title: Cross harness compatibility
docs.text:
This is especially cool for students that juggle several subscriptions and switch the LLM provider as soon as tokens are burned out. APM allows to make it smooth.

graph LR
    subgraph Harnesses
        H_A(Harness A)
        H_B(Harness B)
        H_C(Harness C)
    end

    subgraph User
        Human_A["fa:fa-user User"]
    end

    APM[APM Package]

    Human_A --> H_A
    Human_A --> H_B
    Human_A --> H_C
    APM --> Human_A

Another scenario where cross harness compatibility comes in handy is a team where different people use different harnesses. Maybe less common in companies, but for sure can happen often in academia.

graph LR
    subgraph Harnesses
        H_A(Harness A)
        H_B(Harness B)
        H_C(Harness C)
    end

    subgraph Your dream team
        Human_A["fa:fa-user User A"]
        Human_B["fa:fa-user User B"]
        Human_C["fa:fa-user User C"]
    end

    APM[APM Package]

    Human_A --> H_A
    Human_B --> H_B
    Human_C --> H_C

    APM --> Human_A
    APM --> Human_B
    APM --> Human_C

It is interesting a tool making it easier to switch between harness providers is supported by Microsoft, the company behind Github Copilot.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
with APM setting up a layered package system becomes smooth. We can collaborate with different teams and individuals and depending on the project have access to different packages, some of them can be shared.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Company["Company packages"]
        direction TB
        subgraph Organization["Organization packages"]
            direction TB
            subgraph Team["Team packages"]
                direction TB
                Personal["Personal packages"]
            end
        end
    end

In both industry and academia it is easy to find examples of workflows that are common (like code review) and things that are highly subjective and personal (context of my project, my preferences regarding code, models, format of output, used harness).

docs.title: Governance
docs.text:
graph LR
    Human_A["fa:fa-user User A"]

    subgraph Governance
        Audit
        Scan
        more["and more..."]
    end

    APM[APM Package] --> Governance
    Governance --> Human_A

Another reason that you might want to use APM is the ability to better validate, audit the packages you are using. We do not focus on this are during the workshops.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
graph TD

    subgraph Envs[" "]
        EnvA
        EnvB
    end
    Manifest["manifest"] --> Lockfile["lockfile"]
    Lockfile --> EnvA["Environment A"]
    Lockfile --> EnvB["Environment B"]
    EnvB <-- "parity" --> EnvA

The exact state of the primitives used can be also reproduced. APM has all the elements of a traditional package manager

docs.title: What does an APM package contain?
docs.text:
Let's start with a quick overview of the files, along with a Python analogy. The table below assumes the user knows what uv dependency manager is.

APM component description Python analogy .apm/ dir Stores the raw primitives (skills, agent personas, etc.). src/ dir apm.yml The dependencies definition file. pyproject.toml apm.lock.yml The exact description of dependencies. uv.lock user-name/repo-name Package stored in a GitHub repository. External package stored on PyPi. apm_modules/ Stores all transitive dependencies. Lands here when running apm install. Should be gitignored. .venv/lib/python3.x/site-packages .agents/, .github/skills etc. Place where primitives are deployed (exact location depends on harness). .venv/lib/python3.x/site-packages

docs.title: Add skill
docs.text: Let's see how to add a skill to .apm/!

docs.title: Skills structure
docs.text:
Every skill should follow this directory structure:

.apm/skills/
+-- your-skill/
    +-- SKILL.md           # required: the skill body
    +-- scripts/           # optional: executable scripts (usually python or bash)
    +-- references/        # optional: context the skill loads on demand (e.g. how fix a often occuring bug)
    +-- assets/            # optional: templates, code listings, images, fixtures to be reused
    +-- examples/          # optional: sample inputs and outputs

For more details see the author a skill documentation page.

docs.title: skill frontmatter
docs.text: Frontmatter is a header defining the name and description of our skill, loaded at the beginning of each session. Only if the harness/you decide to use it the whole skill body is loaded. Thus the description is important to align with how the skill is intented to be used.

docs.title: Example frontmatter
docs.text:
---
name: top-stacks
description: Use when user wants the best or most relevant Substack posts for a topic, including requests for reading lists or sources that answer specific questions. Return a ranked top five table of directly linked Substack articles with concise one line relevance notes. DO NOT use it for general web research or recommendations not related to Substacks.
---

Notice that:

  • negative examples are mentioned (less important if you have small number of skills, more important if you have 50+ skills for eliminating conflicts)
  • Use when ... is a good way to start your description.
  • Pay attention to your description, if generated with LLMs it can decrease the user experience.
  • Changing the description is a breaking change.

docs.title: Add agent persona
docs.text:
Warning

Currently APM does not support sub-agents for every harness from the target list. Although Antigravity does support agentic personas. Currently the GitHub issue requesting support for antigravity sub-agents is labelled as deffered.

What is possible to configure?

Key Required name recommended description yes model optional tools optional color optional handoffs optional

Example: 

---
name: latex-compiler
description: Compile LaTeX sources with LuaLaTeX, clean generated files, and diagnose latexmk failures without consuming the parent session's context.
model: mai-code-1.1-flash
tools:
  Read: true
  Grep: true
---

docs.title: Agent persona frontmatter
docs.text: For details regarding agentic personas see agents in APM's primitives catalogue.

docs.title: Add a instruction file
docs.text:
This primitive is handled completly diffrently by copilot and claude.

Key Required Purpose description yes One-line summary; used in compiled context indexes applyTo yes for instructions Glob (or comma-separated globs) the rule binds to

Example:

---
description: Python style rules enforced on src/ and tests/
applyTo: "**/*.py"
---

- Use `pathlib.Path`, never `os.path`.
- Tests live next to the module under `tests/<module>/`.
- ...

When using instructions, remember to run apm compile

docs.title: Drawbacks of using instrucitons
docs.text:
• Very agressive loading
  • People tend to write very long instructions

docs.title: Package layout
docs.text: You have basically two main choices when designing a package: single skill package or a collection of skills. There are of course more options, but this two are the mostly used. See package types for more detaisl.

docs.title: Install a package
docs.text:
Usually I install packages per project using:

apm install user-name/repo-name

For skills that I use across projects all the time I install them globally. Thanks to that I avoid setting this up for every project. Usually I pin the packages using the commit hash to avoid drift.

apm install -g user-name/repo-name

docs.title: Maintanance
docs.text:
• Run apm audit to verify divergence between deployed primitives and your lock file.
  • Run apm prune. This command removes installed packages from apm_modules/ that are neither declared in apm.yml nor retained as transitive nodes in apm.lock.yaml. The command also removes their deployed integration files and updates the lockfile.
  • apm self-update. Update apm to latest version. We recommend to update frequently as the tool is activelly developed.

  1. The most well known primitive are skills, bacause they ususally work as an entry point to more complex workflows. However, there are more of them: agents, instructions, hooks, memory... ↩

docs.title: Hands-on exercise for participants
docs.text: Now it is finally time to get your hands dirty!

docs.title: Path 1: Design a skill for working with LaTeX documents
docs.text:
1. Set up the package repository and install external dependencies.
  2. Work on a skill consisting of multiple primitives.
  3. Learn about the patterns under the hood.

Path 1 can be followed step by step. You do not need to have a custom use case ready.

docs.title: Path 2: Your own package idea
docs.text:
You are on your own regarding the idea! But do not be afraid to ask questions if you need any help.

This list should be helpful when brainstorming and validating your package ideas, especially if this is your first time creating skills.

Hesitating to choose path 2?

We highly recommend this path if you have any experience with building skills as we are open to discussing the design, trade-offs, and implementation details. From our point of view, your real-world use cases are the most interesting to discuss.

docs.title: Goal of the hands-on exercises
docs.text:
1. The exercises are not about writing prompts; skill content is less relevant to us.
  2. The exercise is meant to showcase the benefits of using APM and design patterns.

docs.title: Install APM
docs.text: Follow the instructions to install APM

docs.title: Create a GitHub repo
docs.text:
Create a GitHub repo. It can be private or public. If you plan to share you package with collegues afterwards they must have access to your repository.

Good names are: - my-skill for skingle skill repos, for example research-log-skill - my-team-skills for collection of skills e.g. ml-team-skills

docs.title: Initialize your package
docs.text: apm init

docs.title: Package content ideation
docs.text:
What workflows are good candidates for packaging as a set of agentic primitives?

  1. Internal knowledge and implicit assumptions. Things that the team knows by heart but a new hire would have difficulty to figure out on their own.
  2. Coding standards relevant for given codebase. This is especially useful if you have contributors which computer science is not a major and they are more interested on the end result of the experiment and not necessarily on the type of logger used.
  3. Output format (for example if asked for finding resources output always a table with predefined columns).
  4. Boring multistep workflows (example: generate plot with python script, add to latex with predefined figure styling, compile latex).
  5. Often repeated prompts.

docs.title: What to learn?
docs.text:
• What primitives can I use? See the extensive list of supported primitives.
  • What patterns help with cutting cost, reducing complexity, allowing for use in different projects?

docs.title: Workshop content that may come in handy
docs.text:
• See basic setup for skill repo configuration.
  • Check out the design patterns to select the abstractions.
  • For already existing research codebases, also consider taking a look at the research codebase instrumentation audit. The steps described might help you identify what is worth instrumenting first.

docs.title: Role and capability
docs.text: A read-only academic peer review agent that audits .tex source files for missing citations, ungrounded empirical assertions, and uncited literature claims. It prevents hallucinated citations and accidental text destruction during reviews.

docs.title: File targets and relation
docs.text:
• Target path: .apm/agents/citations-expert.agent.md
  • Primitive relation: Read-only auditor subagent. Operates in a scoped child subagent session configured with non-mutating tools (read, grep).

docs.title: Visual mental model
docs.text:
Allowed Tools: [read, grep]  (No write, replace, or execute)
                 |
                 v
Audit .tex for unsupported declarative claims
                 |
                 v
Output structured actionable comments:
% TODO: [Citation needed] - Provide source for [specific claim].

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
.apm/agents/citations-expert.agent.md:

---
name: citations-expert
description: Reviews .tex files seeking lacking citations. Does NOT add new citations.
tools:
  - read
  - grep
---

You are an expert academic peer reviewer and editor. Your task is to review LaTeX (.tex) source files and identify statements that require citations but currently lack them.

### Citation Criteria (What Needs a Citation)
- Statistics and data not generated by this study.
- Prior work references ("Previous studies show...", "Traditionally...").
- External frameworks, specific software, algorithms, or theories.
- Strong declarative claims that are not common knowledge.

### Output Format
For each missing citation, output a structured actionable block. Do not edit the file directly:

**File:** [Filename]  
**Context:** "...[statement needing citation]..."  
**Reason:** [Why this specific claim requires a source]  
**Suggested LaTeX Comment:** `% TODO: [Citation needed] - Provide source for [specific claim].`

docs.title: Mechanics and execution rules
docs.text:
• Tool sandbox restriction: Grants strictly read and grep permissions. The agent cannot modify files or execute arbitrary bash commands.
  • Citation audit criteria: Targets four explicit failure modes: uncited statistics, generic prior work references, external algorithms/theories, and unsubstantiated claims.
  • Non-destructive commentary output: Produces formatted % TODO: [Citation needed] comments for human authors rather than guessing or hallucinating bibtex references.

docs.title: Architectural reflection: can we do it differently?
docs.text:
• Assumptions: Assumes the author retains authority over citation sources and bibliographic accuracy.
  • Alternative considered (autonomous citation insertion): Allowing the agent to query the web and insert \cite{...} keys directly into manuscripts.
  • Why rejected: Generative LLMs frequently hallucinate fake academic citations or misattribute findings. Allowing unconstrained write access leads to the UNPROMPTED DRIFT anti-pattern. Employing Pattern C2. PERSONA PRELOAD with tool isolation ensures strict read-only auditing, preserving manuscript integrity.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
.apm/skills/compile-pdf/references/commands.md:

# LaTeX Build Commands Reference

Run commands from the directory containing the target.

## build
Build from scratch with LuaLaTeX and latexmk. Always clean the target's generated state and remove its existing PDF before compiling, even when the PDF already exists:

```bash
latexmk -C -emulate-aux-dir -auxdir=build -outdir=. <target> \
  && rm -rf build \
  && rm -f -- <target-basename>.pdf \
  && latexmk -emulate-aux-dir -auxdir=build -outdir=. -f -lualatex -interaction=nonstopmode <target>
```

## clean
Clean auxiliary files while retaining the PDF:

```bash
latexmk -c -emulate-aux-dir -auxdir=build -outdir=. <target>
```

## deep-clean
Remove all latexmk-generated files, then remove the local auxiliary directory:

```bash
latexmk -C -emulate-aux-dir -auxdir=build -outdir=. <target> && rm -rf build
```

docs.title: Key design principles
docs.text:
• Deterministic CLI commands: By centralizing the bash commands (e.g., using latexmk with specific flags for LuaLaTeX), it prevents the LLM from hallucinating incorrect or unpredictable LaTeX build flags during compilation.
  • Path unification: Standardizes the exact shell commands across both the direct-execution fallback path (used by the main skill) and the agent execution path (used by the child persona), guaranteeing consistent behavior regardless of the execution strategy.

docs.title: Compilation engine
docs.text:
The compilation strategy is split into three core primitives. Before implementation, their composition and the necessity of this architectural split are examined.

  1. compile-pdf (Skill facade): The entrypoint skill. It processes user intent, formats a structured task brief, and routes execution either to a child subagent or a direct fallback path.
  2. latex-compiler.agent.md (Persona scoping file): An isolated compiler child persona restricted to executing local shell commands and reading files.
  3. references/commands.md (Shared commands reference): A dedicated reference file standardizing deterministic CLI commands.

docs.title: Justification for architectural split
docs.text:
This separation of concerns addresses several critical issues when dealing with verbose tools like LaTeX compilers:

  • Isolating verbose logs: Running the compiler execution within a child agent prevents verbose compilation logs from polluting the parent conversation context.
  • Clean conversational facade: The entrypoint skill provides a clean conversational interface to the main session and acts as a router.
  • Deterministic commands: Standardizing the build commands ensures that both the direct execution fallback and the agent execution paths use identical commands.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
.apm/skills/compile-pdf/SKILL.md:

---
name: compile-pdf
description: Use this skill when compiling a LaTeX document, rebuilding a PDF, cleaning LaTeX auxiliary files, or diagnosing a failed LuaLaTeX or latexmk build. Use it even when the request mentions only stale output, cache cleanup, or errors from a .tex build.
compatibility: Requires latexmk with LuaLaTeX support for execution.
---

# Compile a LaTeX PDF

You must use the `latex-compiler` agent in a fresh child thread when the runtime can load it with command-execution and file-reading capabilities and return a child receipt. Do not substitute another LaTeX agent or persona. This keeps verbose compiler output out of the parent context. If the `latex-compiler` child cannot be loaded with those capabilities, execute the same protocol directly in the current thread.

## Select the action

- `build`: compile the requested root `.tex` file.
- `clean`: remove auxiliary files but retain the generated PDF.
- `deep-clean`: remove all latexmk-generated files and the local `build` directory.

Identify the root `.tex` target and its containing directory. Use `main.tex` only when the user did not name a target and `main.tex` exists. Do not guess between multiple possible root files.

## Child-thread brief

Pass only this brief to the compiler persona:

```text
ROLE: latex-compiler. RESPOND STRUCTURED ONLY.
ACTION: <build|clean|deep-clean>
TARGET: <relative tex path>
DIRECTORY: <working directory>
BUILD: CLEAN GENERATED STATE AND OLD PDF FIRST, EVEN IF PDF EXISTS.
RUN deterministic command from references/commands.md. VERIFY exit and artifact.
FAIL: parse bounded error digest from build log. NO unrelated edits. NO OTHER PERSONA.
OUTPUT: receipt schema only.
```

Expect this receipt:

```json
{
  "status": "SUCCESS|FAILURE",
  "artifact_path": "<relative PDF path or null>",
  "error_digest": ["<5-10 concise log lines; empty on success>"]
}
```

## Direct execution fallback

Read the exact commands for `build`, `clean`, and `deep-clean` from `references/commands.md`. Run them from the target's containing directory. Reject targets outside the selected directory. Do not replace `build` with a broader path.

## Verify and report

For `build`, report success only when the complete clean-build command exits successfully and the PDF matching the target basename exists and is non-empty. For cleanup, report success only when the command exits successfully.

On failure, inspect the matching log under `build/` when present. Report five to ten relevant diagnostic lines, preserving exact error text, instead of copying the full log. Never return a success-shaped fallback after a failed command.

docs.title: Key design principles
docs.text:
• Structured brief preparation: The skill defines a standardized task brief specifying ROLE, ACTION, TARGET, DIRECTORY, and OUTPUT, keeping child agent initialization concise and predictable.
  • Intelligent routing: The skill acts as a router. It spawns the child compiler subagent if supported by the runtime environment, providing isolation.
  • Direct execution fallback: It provides a direct execution fallback path if subagent spawning is unavailable, ensuring robust execution. Both paths rely on the identical standardized commands reference.

docs.text:
.apm/agents/latex-code-expert.agent.md:

---
name: latex-code-expert
description: Use this agent when reviewing or correcting .tex files for guideline misalignment, LaTeX syntax errors, or formatting violations. Activate when the user reports compile errors, broken table or figure formatting, wrong citation style, or asks for a general LaTeX code review.
tools:
  - read
  - grep
  - write
  - replace
  - latex-table-formatter
  - latex-figure-formatter
---

Before editing any file: re-read the MUST NOT constraints in this brief. Confirm the requested scope. Do not expand beyond it.

Review .tex files seeking misalignment with latex guidelines defined via this APM package or general errors. Your job is to correct the code to ensure it adheres to the guidelines, spelling errors, and is free of latex syntax errors.

### Skills that help with latex formatting:
- latex-table-formatter
- latex-figure-formatter

### What you MUST NOT do
- Do not rewrite any content
- Do not change the structure of the document
- Do not add or remove any sections or paragraphs
- Do not change vocabulary or phrasing
- Do not add or remove any references or citations

docs.title: Mechanics and execution rules
docs.text:
• Composed skill loading: Loads both latex-table-formatter and latex-figure-formatter as sub-skills, allowing the persona to apply canonical package formatting conventions during repair tasks.
  • Negative constraint boundary: Enforces explicit prohibitions ("What you MUST NOT do") against rewriting content, changing structure, modifying vocabulary, or altering citations.
  • Scope discipline: Requires confirming the requested scope before modifying any target .tex file.

docs.title: Architectural reflection: can we do it differently?
docs.text:
• Assumptions: Assumes the user wants automated code and syntax fixes while keeping their original authorial voice untouched.
  • Alternative considered (general coding agent): Using an unconstrained coding agent with standard code editing tools.
  • Why rejected: Unconstrained models frequently rewrite paper prose, change terminology, or reformat headings according to general training priors. Applying Pattern S4. VALIDATION DECORATOR with explicit negative constraints creates a safe mutator boundary, avoiding the UNPROMPTED DRIFT anti-pattern.

docs.title: Role and capability
docs.text: The latex-compiler.agent.md persona is a dedicated child subagent that executes local LaTeX compilation and builds diagnostic error summaries. It acts as an isolated compiler persona.

docs.title: File targets and relation

• Target path: .apm/agents/latex-compiler.agent.md
  • Primitive relation: Spawned child subagent. Invoked exclusively in an isolated thread with restricted tools to perform deterministic CLI actions.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
.apm/agents/latex-compiler.agent.md:

---
name: latex-compiler
description: Compile LaTeX sources with LuaLaTeX, clean generated files, and diagnose latexmk failures without consuming the parent session's context.
tools:
  - execute
  - read
---

You own local LaTeX compilation and cleanup. Work only in the requested directory and do not edit document sources unless the user explicitly asks for a source fix.

## Inputs

Require these values before running a command:

- `action`: `build`, `clean`, or `deep-clean`
- `target`: the root `.tex` file, defaulting to `main.tex` only when it exists
- `directory`: the directory containing the target

## Commands

Use the commands defined in `../skills/compile-pdf/references/commands.md`. Run commands from `directory`. Reject targets outside that directory. Do not substitute a broader path for `build`.

## Verification

For a build, report success only when the complete clean-build command exits successfully and the PDF matching the target basename exists and is non-empty in `directory`. For cleanup, report success only when the command exits successfully.

On failure, inspect the matching log under `build/` when present. Return the five to ten most relevant diagnostic lines, preserving exact error text. Do not return the full log.

## Receipt

Return exactly this structure:

```json
{
  "status": "SUCCESS|FAILURE",
  "artifact_path": "<relative PDF path or null>",
  "error_digest": ["<diagnostic line>"]
}
```

Use an empty `error_digest` on success and a null `artifact_path` when no verified PDF was produced.

docs.title: Key design principles
docs.text:
• Tool constraint boundary: The persona is granted only limited tools (execute and read). It does not possess write or edit tools, ensuring that compilation diagnostics cannot trigger unprompted source rewrites.
  • Structured receipt emission: Returns a strict JSON schema (status, artifact_path, error_digest), allowing the calling skill to verify compilation programmatically.
  • Error digest distillation: When compilation fails, the agent parses the build log and returns only 5 to 10 actionable diagnostic lines rather than dumping massive logs into the parent context.

docs.title: skill body
docs.text:
.apm/skills/latex-figure-formatter/SKILL.md:

---
name: latex-figure-formatter
description: Use this skill when adding or formatting figures (images, diagrams, plots, diagrams) in .tex files. Also activate when the user reports a broken figure reference, a missing caption, a float placement issue, a figure that is too small to read, a missing footnote on a borrowed image, or asks to fix any \begin{figure} environment. Do not use for tables.
---

When adding a figure use the code snippet from [assets](./assets/template_figure_code.tex)

## Main guidelines
- If a figure is inserted it must always be referenced in the text with `\figref{fig:examplePicture}`. Take care to introduce all figures before they show up in text.
- Figures (graphics, pictures, diagrams, ...) are generally inserted centered into the document.
- The figure's description is inserted under it and also centered.
- Labeling figures with the short form \glqq{}Fig.\grqq{} is also possible.
- When inserting graphics, make sure that the text elements contained do not fall below the font size of the body text. 

## Citing a figure
- Figures that were not made by you must generally be marked with footnotes.
- If a figure is modified, say this accordingly (e.g.: Adapted from [original reference]).
- When citing a figure, you need to make sure the footnote is on the same page as the figure itself.
- The footnote defined outside of the figure environment, therefore needs to be placed below or above the figure.

## Mermaid diagrams

For core Mermaid diagram guidelines skills: draw-mermaid and export-mermaid.

    \captionsetup{justification=centering,margin=0cm}
    \caption[This is an example of a figure.]{This is an example of a figure.\protect\footnoteref{fn:Abb1}}
    \label{fig:examplePicture}
\end{figure}
\stepcounter{footnote}\footnotetext{\cite{Lunze2013}, p.~17, fig.~270. \label{fn:Abb1}}

.apm/skills/latex-table-formatter/SKILL.md:

---
name: latex-table-formatter
description: Use this skill when adding or formatting a table in .tex files. Also activate when the user reports misaligned columns, a missing table caption or label, a float placement problem, a table that overflows the page margin, a missing citation footnote on borrowed data, or asks to fix any \begin{tabular} or \begin{table} environment.
---

- Tables are inserted into the document centered.
- The title of the table is positioned over the table and is also centered.
- Labeling tables with the short form \glqq{}Tab.\grqq{} is also possible.
- Numbering is done analogous to figures.
- A table is referenced by using: `\tabref{tab:exampleTable}.`
- Tables that were not made by you (data taken from elsewhere) must generally be marked with footnotes.
- When citing a table, you need to make sure the footnote is on the same page as the figure itself.
- The footnote defined outside of the figure environment, therefore needs to be placed below or above the figure.

You must use the template table from assets: [template table](./assets/template_table_code.tex)

docs.text:
• Alternative considered (inlining): Inlining the full LaTeX table template directly inside the SKILL.md body.
  • Why rejected: As analyzed in the architectural design patterns guide, inlined templates bloat context on every single turn the skill is loaded. Isolating boilerplate into assets/ adheres to Pattern C1. LAZY ASSET and avoids the EAGER BLOAT anti-pattern. Over long research projects, this pattern enables swapping conference/journal/lab/project templates without re-prompting the core formatting logic.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
.apm/skills/latex-workflow/SKILL.md:

---
name: latex-workflow
description: >-
  Use this skill when the user wants to work on a LaTeX document and the
  request spans multiple operations (compile, insert figure, draw diagram,
  create plot, format table, rephrase text) or when the correct specialist
  skill is unclear. Activate on requests like "update my thesis", "fix the
  figure and recompile", "add a Mermaid diagram to my paper and export it",
  or any composite LaTeX authoring task. Does NOT replace individual
  specialist skills when the user's intent is already specific and
  unambiguous.
---

# LaTeX Workflow Orchestrator

Routes composite LaTeX authoring requests to the correct specialist skills
in the correct order. Does not implement any domain logic itself.

## Anchor

Before doing anything, restate:
- The user's goal in one sentence.
- The root `.tex` file (if known).
- Any explicit ordering the user requested.

## 1. Load the dispatch table

Read `assets/dispatch-table.md`.

## 2. Classify intent into tasks

Match the user's request against the intent signals in the dispatch table.
Produce an ordered task list. Apply the ordering rules from the table
(source edits → exports → compile) unless the user specified otherwise.

Write this plan to a `plan.md` file in the document's directory:

```
# LaTeX Workflow Plan
goal: <one sentence>
root: <path to root .tex file, or "not specified">
tasks:
  - id: 1
    skill: <skill-name>
    mode: <spawn | inline>
    description: <what to do>
    status: pending
  - ...
```

If the user's request maps to only ONE task, stop here and delegate
directly to that specialist skill without writing a plan.

## 3. Execute tasks sequentially

For each task in the plan, in order:

**Reload `plan.md` before each task.**

### If mode = spawn

Start a child thread. Pass only this caveman brief:

```
skill: <skill-name>
task: <description from plan>
root: <root .tex path if relevant>
```

Collect the structured receipt. Expected shape:
- `compile-pdf`: `{status, pdf_path, error_summary}`
- `export-mermaid`: `{status, output_paths[]}`

If the child returns an error status, report it immediately and pause.
Ask the user whether to continue, retry, or stop.

### If mode = inline

Load the specialist skill body into the current context and follow its
procedure for the scoped file or text. Do not spawn.

After the inline task completes, update `plan.md` task status to `done`.

## 4. Synthesize

After all tasks are done, emit a brief summary:
- What was done (one bullet per task).
- Any errors or skipped tasks.
- Path to the compiled PDF (if compile-pdf ran).

Do not repeat the full output of each specialist; summarize outcomes only.

.apm/skills/latex-workflow/assets/dispatch-table.md:

# Dispatch Table

Load this asset when classifying the user's intent into individual tasks.

## Dispatch modes

- **inline** — load the specialist skill body into the current thread context and execute there.
- **spawn** — start a fresh child thread seeded with the specialist skill; collect a structured receipt.

## Task → Specialist mapping

| User intent signals | Skill | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| compile, build, rebuild, latexmk, PDF, recompile, clean build, auxiliary files | `compile-pdf` | **spawn** |
| export diagram, render mermaid, mermaid to PNG, mermaid to SVG, mmdc | `export-mermaid` | **spawn** |
| draw diagram, mermaid source, flowchart, sequence diagram, draw mermaid, .mmd | `draw-mermaid` | **inline** |
| insert figure, add figure, add image, add graphic, format figure, figure placement | `latex-figure-formatter` | **inline** |
| insert table, add table, format table, tabular | `latex-table-formatter` | **inline** |
| rephrase, rewrite, LLM-isms, improve phrasing, scientific tone, simplify text | `llm-text-rephrasing` | **inline** |

## Ordering rules

When multiple tasks are identified, sequence them in this order to avoid file conflicts:

1. Source edits first (draw-mermaid, figure, table, rephrase) — modify `.tex` or `.mmd` source.
2. Export next (export-mermaid) — produce image/asset files referenced by `.tex`.
3. Compile last (compile-pdf) — consumes the fully updated source tree.

If the user explicitly specifies an order, honour it.

docs.title: Mechanics and execution rules
docs.text:
• Three-phase execution sequence: Enforces strict execution order:
  • Source edits (inline): draw-mermaid, latex-figure-formatter, latex-table-formatter, llm-text-rephrasing.
  • Asset export (spawn): export-mermaid (runs mmdc to generate PDF/SVG graphics).
  • Compilation (spawn): compile-pdf (executes latexmk LuaLaTeX build once all graphic files exist on disk).
  • Single-task fast-path: When a request involves only one skill, the orchestrator bypasses writing plan.md and hands off execution directly, saving execution overhead.
  • Plan persistence: For composite requests, state is recorded in plan.md, ensuring progress can resume across interruptions.

docs.title: Architectural reflection: can we do it differently?
docs.text:
• Assumptions: Assumes the user requests compound workflows requiring multi-phase coordination.
  • Alternative considered (monolithic all-in-one skill): Packing all table, figure, mermaid, rephrasing, and compilation instructions into a single massive orchestrator prompt.
  • Why rejected: As covered in the architectural design patterns guide, an all-in-one skill embodies the GOD MODULE and ALL-BRANCHES-LOADED anti-patterns. By implementing Pattern S3. ORCHESTRATOR FACADE and Pattern B2. CONDITIONAL DISPATCH, latex-workflow remains a lean dispatcher that dynamically invokes specialist primitives only when needed. It avoids STUB ORCHESTRATION by enforcing strict phase ordering and state verification.

docs.title: Path 1: Design your LaTeX package step by step
docs.text:
In this exercise, we build an APM package, similar to latex-skills. The goal is to separate the LaTeX workflow into clear specialist skills and an orchestrator that keeps the primary conversation session compact.

By the end of the chapter, you will understand how a LaTeX package routes figure and table edits, Mermaid exports, prose polishing, and PDF compilation without pooling all rules into a single monolithic skill.

docs.title: Motivation: why an agentic LaTeX workflow?
docs.text:
• Repetitive toil: Academic writing repeatedly cycles through table formatting, figure insertion, citation checks, and compilation failures.
  • Standardized conventions: Conference templates are consistent enough to encode as reusable execution rules.

docs.title: Architecture overview and theory cross-references
docs.text:

docs.title: Architectural design patterns used
docs.text:
Before authoring primitives, review how the package maps to the patterns and anti-patterns defined in the architectural design patterns guide:

Pattern name Where used? Why used? R1. SPLIT Package architecture across latex-skills Decomposes a monolithic prompt into independent specialist skills and an orchestrator. S3. ORCHESTRATOR FACADE latex-workflow Exposes a single entrypoint while coordinating multi-step execution behind the scenes. B2. CONDITIONAL DISPATCH latex-workflow dispatch table Classifies intent to load only the relevant skill instead of loading all rules at once. C3. THREAD SPAWN compile-pdf Runs noisy compilation in an isolated child thread that returns only a compact receipt. C1. LAZY ASSET latex-table-formatter and latex-figure-formatter Stores LaTeX templates in external asset files, loading them into context only on demand. S7. DETERMINISTIC TOOL BRIDGE latex-compiler Bridges agent intent to deterministic CLI commands (latexmk, lualatex) S4. VALIDATION DECORATOR latex-compiler receipt verification Enforces deterministic pass/fail gates and concise error digests before returning to the parent. C2. PERSONA PRELOAD citations-expert, latex-code-expert, and latex-compiler Scopes execution roles with specialized instructions and restricted toolsets for each persona.

docs.title: Architectural anti-patterns avoided
docs.text: Anti-pattern name Where avoided? Why avoided? GOD MODULE Across the overall package structure Prevents combining routing, formatting, and compiling in one unmaintainable prompt. ALL-BRANCHES-LOADED In latex-workflow Prevents inflating prompt tokens with rules for all skills when only one is required. FAN-OUT-IN-ONE-CONTEXT In compile-pdf Prevents flooding the parent conversation with tokens of verbose compiler log noise. EAGER BLOAT In latex-table-formatter Prevents inlining large LaTeX template blocks directly inside SKILL.md bodies. STUB ORCHESTRATION In latex-workflow Avoids a pass-through wrapper by introducing interlock, gate, synthesis and doesn't block direct skill invocations. TOOLLESS ASSERTION In latex-compiler Prevents hallucinating build status without actually executing the compiler CLI. WRAPPING WITHOUT BLOCKING In latex-compiler diagnostics Halts downstream tasks immediately upon build errors instead of proceeding silently.

docs.title: Initialize the package repository
docs.text:
Following the APM workflow established in the basic setup and installation walkthrough, create a directory named latex-skills:

mkdir latex-skills && cd latex-skills

Initialize it with APM:

apm init

docs.title: Declare external dependencies
docs.text:
The canonical package does not rebuild Mermaid rendering or rephrasing logic from scratch. It reuses external APM packages and keeps its own package focused on LaTeX orchestration and formatting, aligning with the composability principles in the package organization guide:

apm install KTFish/llm-text-rephrasing-skills#v0.2.0
apm install KTFish/mermaid-skills#v0.2.0

This yields an apm.yml configuration:

name: latex-skills
version: 0.1.0
description: Skills for efficient LaTeX document development.
targets:
  - copilot
  - gemini
  - antigravity
  - claude
dependencies:
  apm:
    - KTFish/llm-text-rephrasing-skills#v0.2.0
    - KTFish/mermaid-skills#v0.2.0
  mcp: []
includes: auto

The package name and the exposed skill name can differ: KTFish/llm-text-rephrasing-skills exposes the skill named llm-text-rephrasing, while mermaid-skills contributes both draw-mermaid and export-mermaid.

Primitive relation: external packages

External dependencies like KTFish/mermaid-skills and KTFish/llm-text-rephrasing-skills illustrate the external package relation type. Rather than duplicating diagram rendering or tone auditing in latex-skills, the package imports them as pinned upstream dependencies.

docs.title: Configure execution targets
docs.text:
As discussed in the package organization guide, the targets field determines where APM integrates primitives across different agent harnesses. 1

targets:
  - copilot
  - gemini
  - antigravity
  - claude

Running apm install then deploys primitives into target-specific locations, such as .agents/skills/ for Antigravity and .github/skills/ for Copilot.

We recommend starting with a single target (e.g. the harness you use most frequently) to avoid confusion. More targets can always be added later.

docs.title: Host dependencies
docs.text:
In case of installation issues

In case of installation issues skip this step, as it is not the most important step to understand the core concepts relevant for the workshops. Installation of system level dependencies (latex, mermaid) can be finished latter on.

docs.title: Mermaid CLI
docs.text:
Install Mermaid CLI to compile and render Mermaid diagrams, especially .mmd files converted to .pdf or .svg:

Mac / Linux: 

brew install mermaid-cli

Windows: 

npm install -g @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli

docs.title: LaTeX compilation (LuaLaTeX + latexmk)
docs.text:
Mac: 

brew install --cask mactex

Linux: 

sudo apt-get install texlive-full latexmk

Windows: 

winget install MiKTeX.MiKTeX

  1. When initializing a package, APM prompts for target platforms. While environments like copilot, gemini, and claude can be selected during interactive initialization, configure antigravity by adding it directly to the targets list in apm.yml: ↩

docs.title: Patterns vs anti-patterns comparison
docs.text:
Let's take a quick look on the desing patterns and issues we avoided by using them

Primitive Design Pattern Applied Anti-Pattern Prevented Trade-off / Justification latex-workflow S3. ORCHESTRATOR FACADE & B2. CONDITIONAL DISPATCH GOD MODULE & ALL-BRANCHES-LOADED Separates orchestration from domain execution; keeps individual skills modular and inspectable. compile-pdf / latex-compiler C3. THREAD SPAWN & S7. DETERMINISTIC TOOL BRIDGE FAN-OUT-IN-ONE-CONTEXT & TOOLLESS ASSERTION Sequesters thousands of lines of compiler logs in a child thread and verifies build exit status. latex-figure-formatter / latex-table-formatter C1. LAZY ASSET EAGER BLOAT Moves TeX templates to assets/, reducing prompt token consumption until explicitly needed and allowing for adding more templates in future. citations-expert C2. PERSONA PRELOAD UNPROMPTED DRIFT Agent is strictly read-only (read, grep), preventing accidental or hallucinated manuscript revisions. latex-code-expert S4. VALIDATION DECORATOR UNPROMPTED DRIFT Constrained mutator bounded by explicit negative rules preventing unauthorized prose alterations. add-plot skill removed R1. SPLIT (Boundary Discipline) GOD MODULE (Scope Creep) In an early version of the latex-skill package it contained a skill for handling matplotlib plots. Python plot generation was decoupled from a latex focussed package thus skipped in the workshops.

docs.title: Hands-on testing
docs.text:
Test your package on a real LaTeX document!

Ideas of what you can do: 1. Translate a markdown document into latex, then compile to pdf. 2. Draw a mermaid diagram illustrating content of a paragraph and add it to your doc.

docs.text:
That was it! Thank you for participating in the workshops.

In this section we list the sources used in this tutorial as well as further steps that might interest you. We hope you have enjoyed the workshops, please consider to provide feedback via the form

Did we miss anything cool in this list? Feel free to open an issue!

docs.title: Genesis
docs.text:
• Genesis design patterns catalogue.
  • It is wrapped into a skill that helps with desingning your agentic primitives.
    • Hint 1: Read the catalogue first, the skill uses a lot of jargon. You will benefit way more if you are familiarized with the concepts before using it.
    • Hint 2: Ask directly for using APM.

docs.title: Research repos
docs.text:
The way we code nowadays shifted significantly. I personally believe that there are no more excuses for researchers publishing papers with code that makes it hard to reproduce. Defining the standards a single time is a low cost paid once, from which every subsequent paper benefits.

The table below tries to confront the existing challenges with feasible solutions, that were not possible few years ago.

research repo issue current solution via codebase instrumentation no idea why we did it this way Use a research log, add primitives that activelly transform your dirty comments, commits, noteboks into a structured log reviews unfeasible, hard to extract the important information from huge pr define standards upfront, allow reviewers to focus on the research meat only no time for refactors define patterns upfront, avoid post cleanup not enough time for maintenance setup automatic workflows for simple maintenance tasks

docs.title: Mentoring in the age of slop
docs.text:
Professors have the precious judgment. When building appropriate primitives this judgement can be used effectively, not only by themself but by PHDs and students.

On the other hand the preceptorship model proposed by Microsoft suits also research environments. A Preceptorship is a structured, individualized teaching and mentoring period where an experienced professional guides a student or newly licensed worker in a real-world setting. The new model must allow both seniors (profs) and juniors (students), experienced alongside early in career, to learn, not just produce. Senior (prof, PHDs) mentors should assess weaknesses and guide focus areas, while AI serves as an accelerant, not a crutch.

docs.title: [Optional] Upload generated skill to Claude App
docs.text: This step is optional but highly useful for often repeated workflows that you run from your phone. I like to use this for tasks unrelated to coding like searching and organizing information in formats I like.
